claim: Mutations altering the scaffolding protein Shank are linked to several psychiatric disorders.
source: Mutations altering the scaffolding protein Shank are linked to several psychiatric disorders, and to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Mutations altering the scaffolding protein Shank are linked to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice.
source: Mutations altering the scaffolding protein Shank are linked to several psychiatric disorders, and to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Shank directly binds CaV1 voltage activated calcium channels.
source: Among its many binding partners, Shank directly binds CaV1 voltage activated calcium channels.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and by prior work from the authors.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans SHN-1/Shank promotes CaV1 coupling to calcium activated potassium channels.
source: Here, we show that the Caenorhabditis elegans SHN-1/Shank promotes CaV1 coupling to calcium activated potassium channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations inactivating SHN-1 increase action potential durations in body muscles.
source: Mutations inactivating SHN-1, and those preventing SHN-1 binding to EGL-19/CaV1 all increase action potential durations in body muscles.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mutations preventing SHN-1 binding to EGL-19/CaV1 increase action potential durations in body muscles.
source: Mutations inactivating SHN-1, and those preventing SHN-1 binding to EGL-19/CaV1 all increase action potential durations in body muscles.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Action potential repolarization is mediated by two classes of potassium channels: SHK-1/KCNA and SLO-1 and SLO-2 BK channels.
source: Action potential repolarization is mediated by two classes of potassium channels: SHK-1/KCNA and SLO-1 and SLO-2 BK channels.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4 showing effects of mutations in these channels.

claim: BK channels are calcium-dependent.
source: BK channels are calcium-dependent, and their activation requires tight coupling to EGL-19/CaV1 channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BK channels and is supported by experiments in Figure 7.

claim: BK channel activation requires tight coupling to EGL-19/CaV1 channels.
source: BK channels are calcium-dependent, and their activation requires tight coupling to EGL-19/CaV1 channels.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using calcium chelators and channel antagonists in Figure 7.

claim: SHN-1's effects on AP duration are mediated by changes in BK channels.
source: SHN-1's effects on AP duration are mediated by changes in BK channels.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments in Figure 6 showing that slo-2 mutations block SHN-1's effects.

claim: In shn-1 mutants, SLO-2 currents are significantly decreased in both body muscles and neurons.
source: In shn-1 mutants, SLO-2 currents and channel clustering are significantly decreased in both body muscles and neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: In shn-1 mutants, SLO-2 channel clustering is significantly decreased in both body muscles and neurons.
source: In shn-1 mutants, SLO-2 currents and channel clustering are significantly decreased in both body muscles and neurons.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: Increased and decreased shn-1 gene copy number produce similar changes in AP width.
source: Finally, increased and decreased shn-1 gene copy number produce similar changes in AP width and SLO-2 current.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in Figure 8 comparing animals with 1, 2, and 4 copies of shn-1.

claim: Increased and decreased shn-1 gene copy number produce similar changes in SLO-2 current.
source: Finally, increased and decreased shn-1 gene copy number produce similar changes in AP width and SLO-2 current.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in Figure 8 comparing animals with 1, 2, and 4 copies of shn-1.

claim: An important function of Shank is to promote microdomain coupling of BK with CaV1.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that an important function of Shank is to promote microdomain coupling of BK with CaV1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including calcium chelator experiments.

claim: Shank is a synaptic scaffolding protein containing SH3, PDZ, proline-rich and SAM domains.
source: Shank is a synaptic scaffolding protein (containing SH3, PDZ, proline-rich and SAM domains) (Grabrucker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Shank protein structure supported by citation.

claim: Mammals have three Shank genes, each encoding multiple isoforms.
source: Mammals have three Shank genes, each encoding multiple isoforms (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mouse Shank knockouts exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects.
source: Several mouse Shank knockouts have been described but these mutants exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013), most likely resulting from differences in the Shank isoforms impacted by each mutation.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a summary of prior literature.

claim: The inconsistent phenotypes in mouse Shank knockouts most likely result from differences in the Shank isoforms impacted by each mutation.
source: Several mouse Shank knockouts have been described but these mutants exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013), most likely resulting from differences in the Shank isoforms impacted by each mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of inconsistent phenotypes.

claim: The biochemical mechanism by which Shank mutations alter synaptic function and behavior has not been determined.
source: The biochemical mechanism by which Shank mutations alter synaptic function and behavior has not been determined.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) in humans.
source: In humans, Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), schizophrenia, and mania (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to schizophrenia in humans.
source: In humans, Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), schizophrenia, and mania (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to mania in humans.
source: In humans, Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), schizophrenia, and mania (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: Haploinsufficiency for 22q13 (which spans the Shank3 locus) occurs in Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS).
source: Haploinsufficiency for 22q13 (which spans the Shank3 locus) occurs in Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), a syndromic form of ASD (Phelan and McDermid, 2012).

claim: Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS) is a syndromic form of ASD.

claim: PMS patients exhibit autistic behaviors accompanied by hypotonia, delayed speech, and intellectual disability (ID).
source: PMS patients exhibit autistic behaviors accompanied by hypotonia, delayed speech, and intellectual disability (ID) (Bonaglia et al., 2011).

claim: Heterozygous inactivating Shank3 mutations are found in sporadic ASD and schizophrenia.
source: Heterozygous inactivating Shank3 mutations are found in sporadic ASD and schizophrenia (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).

claim: 22q13 duplications spanning Shank3 are found in ASD, schizophrenia, ADHD, and bipolar disorder.
source: 22q13 duplications spanning Shank3 are found in ASD, schizophrenia, ADHD, and bipolar disorder (Durand et al., 2007; Failla et al., 2007; Han et al., 2013).

claim: A transgenic mouse that selectively over-expresses Shank3 exhibits hyperactive behavior and susceptibility to seizures.
source: A transgenic mouse that selectively over-expresses Shank3 exhibits hyperactive behavior and susceptibility to seizures (Han et al., 2013).

claim: Too little or too much Shank3 can contribute to the pathophysiology underlying psychiatric disorders.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that too little or too much Shank3 can contribute to the pathophysiology underlying these psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited genetic and mouse studies.

claim: Shank is highly enriched in the post-synaptic densities of excitatory synapses.
source: Shank is highly enriched in the post-synaptic densities of excitatory synapses; consequently, most studies have focused on the idea that Shank proteins regulate some aspect of synapse formation or function.

claim: Most studies have focused on the idea that Shank proteins regulate some aspect of synapse formation or function.
source: Shank is highly enriched in the post-synaptic densities of excitatory synapses; consequently, most studies have focused on the idea that Shank proteins regulate some aspect of synapse formation or function.

claim: Shank proteins bind many proteins through its various domains.

source: Shank mutations decrease the synaptic localization of NMDA and AMPA type glutamate receptors (Peça et al., 2011; Won et al., 2012).

claim: Shank proteins promote delivery of HCN channels to the plasma membrane.
source: Other studies show that Shank proteins promote delivery of several ion channels to the plasma membrane, including HCN channels (Yi et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2018), TRPV channels (Han et al., 2016), and CaV1 voltage activated calcium channels (Pym et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Shank proteins promote delivery of TRPV channels to the plasma membrane.
source: Other studies show that Shank proteins promote delivery of several ion channels to the plasma membrane, including HCN channels (Yi et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2018), TRPV channels (Han et al., 2016), and CaV1 voltage activated calcium channels (Pym et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Shank proteins promote delivery of CaV1 voltage activated calcium channels to the plasma membrane.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Human CACNA1C (which encodes a CaV1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD.
source: Of these potential binding partners, we focus on CaV1 because human CACNA1C (which encodes a CaV1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD (Splawski et al., 2005; Splawski et al., 2004), and polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders (Psychiatric Genomics, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders.
source: Of these potential binding partners, we focus on CaV1 because human CACNA1C (which encodes a CaV1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD (Splawski et al., 2005; Splawski et al., 2004), and polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders (Psychiatric Genomics, 2013).

claim: C. elegans has a single Shank gene, shn-1.
source: C. elegans has a single Shank gene, shn-1.

claim: The SHN-1 protein lacks an SH3 domain but has all other domains found in mammalian Shank proteins.
source: The SHN-1 protein lacks an SH3 domain but has all other domains found in mammalian Shank proteins.
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on sequence analysis.

claim: Mammalian Shank proteins directly bind CaV1 channels through both the SH3 and PDZ domains.
source: Mammalian Shank proteins directly bind CaV1 channels through both the SH3 and PDZ domains (Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: The SHN-1 PDZ domain directly binds to a carboxy-terminal ligand in EGL-19/CaV1.
source: We previously showed that the SHN-1 PDZ domain directly binds to a carboxy-terminal ligand in EGL-19/CaV1 (Pym et al., 2017).

claim: CaV1 channels are tightly coupled to multiple downstream calcium activated pathways.
source: CaV1 channels are tightly coupled to multiple downstream calcium activated pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaV1 channel function.

claim: C. elegans and mouse Shank proteins promote CaV1-mediated activation of the transcription factor CREB.
source: C. elegans and mouse Shank proteins have been shown to promote CaV1-mediated activation of the transcription factor CREB (Perfitt et al., 2020; Pym et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BK channels are activated by both membrane depolarization and by cytoplasmic calcium.
source: BK channels are activated by both membrane depolarization and by cytoplasmic calcium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BK channel biophysics.

claim: At resting cytoplasmic calcium levels (~100 nM), BK channels have extremely low open probability.
source: At resting cytoplasmic calcium levels (~100 nM), BK channels have extremely low open probability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BK channel biophysics.

claim: BK channels bind calcium with a Kd ranging from 1 to 10 μM.
source: BK channels bind calcium with a Kd ranging from 1 to 10 μM (Contreras et al., 2013); consequently, efficient BK channel activation requires tight spatial coupling to voltage activated calcium (CaV) channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Efficient BK channel activation requires tight spatial coupling to voltage activated calcium (CaV) channels.
source: BK channels bind calcium with a Kd ranging from 1 to 10 μM (Contreras et al., 2013); consequently, efficient BK channel activation requires tight spatial coupling to voltage activated calcium (CaV) channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium binding affinity and resting calcium levels.

claim: BK channels associate with all classes of CaV channels.
source: BK channels associate with all classes of CaV channels (Berkefeld et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: The co-clustering of BK and CaV channels allows rapid activation of hyperpolarizing potassium currents following depolarization.
source: The co-clustering of BK and CaV channels allows rapid activation of hyperpolarizing potassium currents following depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional coupling of these channels.

claim: BK channels decrease action potential (AP) durations in neurons and muscles.
source: BK channels decrease action potential (AP) durations, promote rapid after hyperpolarization potentials, decrease the duration of calcium entry, and limit secretion of neurotransmitters and hormones in neurons and muscles (Adams et al., 1982; Edgerton and Reinhart, 2003; Petersen and Maruyama, 1984; Storm, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BK channels promote rapid after hyperpolarization potentials in neurons and muscles.
source: BK channels decrease action potential (AP) durations, promote rapid after hyperpolarization potentials, decrease the duration of calcium entry, and limit secretion of neurotransmitters and hormones in neurons and muscles (Adams et al., 1982; Edgerton and Reinhart, 2003; Petersen and Maruyama, 1984; Storm, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BK channels decrease the duration of calcium entry in neurons and muscles.
source: BK channels decrease action potential (AP) durations, promote rapid after hyperpolarization potentials, decrease the duration of calcium entry, and limit secretion of neurotransmitters and hormones in neurons and muscles (Adams et al., 1982; Edgerton and Reinhart, 2003; Petersen and Maruyama, 1984; Storm, 1987).

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BK channels have profound effects on circuit activity.
source: Thus, BK channels have profound effects on circuit activity.

source: C. elegans has two BK channel subunits (SLO-1 and SLO-2), both of which form calcium and voltage dependent potassium channels when heterologously expressed (Wang et al., 2001; Yuan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both SLO-1 and SLO-2 form calcium and voltage dependent potassium channels when heterologously expressed.
source: C. elegans has two BK channel subunits (SLO-1 and SLO-2), both of which form calcium and voltage dependent potassium channels when heterologously expressed (Wang et al., 2001; Yuan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SLO-2 channels are also activated by cytoplasmic chloride.
source: SLO-2 channels are also activated by cytoplasmic chloride (Yuan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Neuronal SLO-1 and –2 channels inhibit neurotransmitter release.
source: As in mammals, neuronal SLO-1 and –2 channels inhibit neurotransmitter release (Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2007; Sancar et al., 2011), presumably via their coupling to UNC-2/CaV2 and EGL-19/CaV1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Neuronal SLO-1 and –2 channels inhibit neurotransmitter release presumably via their coupling to UNC-2/CaV2 and EGL-19/CaV1.
source: As in mammals, neuronal SLO-1 and –2 channels inhibit neurotransmitter release (Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2007; Sancar et al., 2011), presumably via their coupling to UNC-2/CaV2 and EGL-19/CaV1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of BK channel function.

claim: In body muscles, SLO-1 channels are co-localized with EGL-19/CaV1 channels.

claim: In body muscles, SLO-1 channels regulate muscle excitability and behavior.

claim: SHN-1 promotes BK coupling to EGL-19/CaV1 channels, thereby decreasing AP duration.

claim: EGL-19/CaV1 channels mediate the primary depolarizing current during body muscle APs.
source: EGL-19/CaV1 channels mediate the primary depolarizing current during body muscle APs (Jospin et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In WT animals, body muscles exhibit a pattern of spontaneous AP bursts (~10 APs/burst; burst frequency 0.1 Hz).
source: In WT animals, body muscles exhibit a pattern of spontaneous AP bursts (~10 APs/burst; burst frequency 0.1 Hz) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Within a burst, APs became progressively wider.
source: Within a burst, APs became progressively wider (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A similar pattern of progressive AP broadening during burst firing has been reported for many neurons.
source: A similar pattern of progressive AP broadening during burst firing has been reported for many neurons (Geiger and Jonas, 2000; Jackson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Outward potassium currents were progressively decreased during repetitive depolarization.
source: Outward potassium currents were progressively decreased during repetitive depolarization (Figure 1C), suggesting that progressive AP broadening most likely results from accumulation of inactivated potassium channels during bursts, as seen in other cell types (Geiger and Jonas, 2000; Kole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Progressive AP broadening most likely results from accumulation of inactivated potassium channels during bursts.
source: Outward potassium currents were progressively decreased during repetitive depolarization (Figure 1C), suggesting that progressive AP broadening most likely results from accumulation of inactivated potassium channels during bursts, as seen in other cell types (Geiger and Jonas, 2000; Kole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in potassium currents and comparison to other cell types.

claim: WT muscles occasionally exhibit prolonged depolarizations (>150ms), which are designated plateau potentials (PPs).
source: Occasionally, WT muscles also exhibited prolonged depolarizations ( > 150ms), which are hereafter designated plateau potentials (PPs).
evidence: This is a definition based on observed data.

claim: PPs often occur at the end of an AP burst.
source: PPs often occur at the end of an AP burst (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate is significantly increased compared to WT.
source: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate and AP widths were significantly increased, AP amplitudes were decreased, resting membrane potential (RMP) was depolarized, while AP frequency and input resistance were unaltered (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, AP widths are significantly increased compared to WT.
source: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate and AP widths were significantly increased, AP amplitudes were decreased, resting membrane potential (RMP) was depolarized, while AP frequency and input resistance were unaltered (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, AP amplitudes are decreased compared to WT.
source: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate and AP widths were significantly increased, AP amplitudes were decreased, resting membrane potential (RMP) was depolarized, while AP frequency and input resistance were unaltered (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, resting membrane potential (RMP) is depolarized compared to WT.
source: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate and AP widths were significantly increased, AP amplitudes were decreased, resting membrane potential (RMP) was depolarized, while AP frequency and input resistance were unaltered (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, AP frequency is unaltered compared to WT.
source: In shn-1 null mutants, PP rate and AP widths were significantly increased, AP amplitudes were decreased, resting membrane potential (RMP) was depolarized, while AP frequency and input resistance were unaltered (Figure 1D–I).

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, input resistance is unaltered compared to WT.

claim: Similar increases in AP widths and PP rate were observed in three, independently derived shn-1 null mutants (nu712, nu652, and tm488).
source: Similar increases in AP widths and PP rate were observed in three, independently derived shn-1 null mutants (nu712, nu652, and tm488) (Table 1).

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing studies suggest that SHN-1 is expressed in muscles, neurons, glia, and epithelial cells.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing studies suggest that SHN-1 is expressed in muscles, neurons, glia, and epithelial cells (Cao et al., 2017; Packer et al., 2019), consistent with the broad expression of split GFP tagged shn-1(nu600 GFP11) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The broad expression of split GFP tagged shn-1(nu600 GFP11) is consistent with single-cell RNA sequencing studies.

evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AP widths and PP frequency were increased in shn-1(muscle KO).

claim: The defect in AP widths and PP frequency in shn-1(muscle KO) was eliminated in shn-1(muscle rescue).
source: Using these alleles, we found that AP widths and PP frequency were increased in shn-1(muscle Knockout, KO) and that this defect was eliminated in shn-1(muscle rescue) (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: shn-1(neuron KO) had no effect on PP rate or AP widths.
source: By contrast, shn-1(neuron KO) and shn-1(neuron rescue) had no effect on PP rate or AP widths (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: shn-1(neuron rescue) had no effect on PP rate or AP widths.
source: By contrast, shn-1(neuron KO) and shn-1(neuron rescue) had no effect on PP rate or AP widths (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: CRE expression in muscles produced opposite changes in AP firing patterns in strains containing the shn-1 nu697 and nu652 alleles.

claim: The PP rate and AP width defects observed in shn-1(muscle KO) were not significantly different from those in shn-1(null).
source: The PP rate and AP width defects observed in shn-1(muscle KO) were not significantly different from those in shn-1(null) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: SHN-1 acts in body muscles to control AP duration.

claim: PP frequency was significantly increased by a deletion removing the EGL-19 carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand [egl-19(nu496 ΔVTTL)].

claim: AP widths were significantly increased by a deletion removing the SHN-1 PDZ domain [shn-1(nu542 ΔPDZ)].
